clue.text: Pitched battle by river with fire-raiser ?

parts.note: the Test is a river in Hampshire, a crossword favourite
a match is what raises a fire, playfully a fire-raiser rather than an arsonist

explanation.surface: A riverside fight breaks out involving an arsonist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitched' looks like it describes a fierce fight; in fact the contest is played on a cricket pitch. A TEST MATCH is an international cricket game lasting up to five days.
explanation.definitionFit: An international cricket fixture is a battle fought out on a pitch.

parts.note: tall and high both mean of great height
an order is a command

explanation.surface: A demanding task is handed down from the top brass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High Command' reads as the military leadership, but splits into two separate words for the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An unreasonably demanding request or task is an idiom for something hard to fulfil.

indicators.note: the letters of was are made different by rearranging them

parts.note: in means at home, as in staying in

explanation.surface: Someone's partner behaved unusually around the house.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints a domestic scene; 'at home' is the stock crossword sense of IN, as in 'staying in'.
explanation.definitionFit: A swain is an old poetic word for a young male suitor or sweetheart.

parts.note: a man is someone, a person
to drill is to train soldiers by repetition

explanation.surface: A keeper is sought who can train a creature.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an animal trainer; the pieces are a person and the verb for military training.
explanation.definitionFit: A large West African baboon with a vividly coloured face is a primate.

clue.text: Doing well to put French rine in right order

indicators.note: putting letters in a new order means rearranging them

parts.note: vin is French for wine, the vine's product

explanation.surface: A grower prospers by arranging his French vines properly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put ... in right order' says put VIN in with RIGHT and rearrange the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Prospering or flourishing describes someone or something doing well.

clue.text: Messenger for one involved… in arms control

explanation.surface: An envoy is engaged in disarmament talks.
explanation.definitionFit: A herald carried official proclamations; heralds also regulate coats of arms, granting and recording armorial bearings.

explanation.surface: Someone is scurrying about inside the music.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket the tally of runs is the side's total; a written-out piece of music, with every part, is also called this.

clue.text: Taking one's part in railway construction

explanation.surface: Someone is doing their share of building the railway.
explanation.definitionFit: Supporting someone in a dispute is backing them; a short track off the main line where trains are parked has the same name.

clue.text: Poor patient losing extremities, .perhaps, in this

definitions.text: Poor patient losing extremities, .perhaps, in this

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters could form something else, so they are rearranged
losing extremities means the first and last letters of patient are dropped

explanation.surface: A sick person may end up losing limbs during surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: POOR plus ATIEN ('patient' without its first and last letters) are rearranged, 'perhaps' signalling the anagram; the whole clue describes surgery where an amputation might happen.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgery is where a patient might have limbs removed, so the whole clue describes a surgical procedure.

clue.text: With some success, a youth's to have a go

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A young person tries something, with partial success.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'success, a', with the comma ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: To essay is an old verb meaning to attempt or try something.

parts.note: L, from the Latin libra, is the abbreviation for a pound sterling
someone who is paid for work is a wage earner

explanation.surface: A student is handed a pound for some work.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'paid a pound' as 'one who earns an L'. L is also the plate on a British learner driver's car.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyone still being taught, at a desk or behind the wheel, is a novice studying a skill.

explanation.surface: Soldiers are given money in place of a new uniform.
explanation.definitionFit: Making good a wrong is reparation; split as RED DRESS it is the scarlet ceremonial outfit of the British army.

clue.text: He has new alloy coated with gold

indicators.note: something coated with a metal is wrapped round by it, so the gold letters go outside

parts.note: OR is the heraldic word for gold

indicators.note: an alloy is a mixture of metals, so the letters of new are mixed up

explanation.surface: A man has a fresh metal mixture plated with gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alloy' looks like a noun in a metalwork scene but acts as the anagram signal; 'He has' as a definition means the one who possesses.
explanation.definitionFit: A possessor is the person who has something, so 'he has' describes a proprietor.

explanation.surface: Organ music in church is played without obligation.
explanation.definitionFit: An organ solo before or after a service bears this name; anything done of one's own free will, without payment or compulsion, is so described.

parts.note: de is the French word for of, so of in a foreign tongue
filing papers is routine clerical office work

explanation.surface: Someone exposes sleaze within the British Foreign Office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foreign Office' reads as the British government department, but the phrase splits after 'of', which pairs with 'Foreign' as French.
explanation.definitionFit: To defile something is to pollute or sully it, so the act is a corruption.

parts.note: a facet is one aspect or view of a subject
IOUs are written promises to pay debts

explanation.surface: A joking opinion is offered on the subject of money owed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' just joins the pieces: in a down clue, the debts sit on (below) the view.
explanation.definitionFit: Being flippantly humorous or joking inappropriately is the same as being jocose.

explanation.surface: A sports venue is being run by the top competitor.
explanation.definitionFit: A boxing venue is a square roped space; at a wedding the groom's chief attendant keeps hold of the band until the vows.

parts.note: green means fresh, new or unripe
a gage is an old word for a pledge or security

explanation.surface: A new promise to provide fruit is made.
explanation.walkthrough: GAGE is an archaic word for something left as security, also a thrown-down challenge.
explanation.definitionFit: A greengage is a sweet green variety of plum.

parts.note: refers to the British idiom for ostracising someone: they are sent to a certain Midlands city and nobody speaks to them

explanation.surface: A letter went somewhere without an address on it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as post sent without an address. 'Sent to Coventry', a British idiom, means deliberately ignored, never spoken to.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sent to the West Midlands city is the British idiom for being shunned and not spoken to.

clue.text: US general's sound medical report-good one

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, linking definition and wordplay

indicators.note: sound tells us the answer is pronounced like the phrase that follows

parts.note: a good bulletin on a patient would say they are still well

explanation.surface: An American general receives a healthy medical report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like it means healthy but signals a homophone. Joseph 'Vinegar Joe' Stilwell commanded US forces in China and Burma in the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Stilwell was an American four-star army commander in the China-Burma-India theatre.

clue.text: Stretcher cases put here when travelling

explanation.surface: Injured passengers on stretchers are stowed away on a journey.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval torture frame stretched its victims; on trains, luggage goes on the overhead shelf.

clue.text: Hint to carry on — can mean just that

indicators.note: the hint word holds or carries the next pieces within it

parts.note: a cue is a hint or prompt to act
taken as written
a tin is a can

explanation.surface: A prompt to keep going may mean exactly what it says.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points back: the result can mean 'carry on'. So 'to carry' does the container work while 'mean just that' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep going is to proceed without stopping, which is just what 'carry on' says.

parts.note: a church assistant to the vicar, though read as edge plus man the name sounds like one who stands at the side

explanation.surface: A clergyman's assistant who is not a churchwarden's deputy.
explanation.walkthrough: A sideman is a churchwarden's assistant. The pun: a verge is a side or edge, so a VERGE-R would be a 'sideman' after all, despite the question.
explanation.definitionFit: A church official who looks after the building and leads processions is an assistant to the vicar.

explanation.surface: A question about a delay for a member following procedure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold-up' suggests a delay but is a band that holds things up; 'member' is a limb, and also a member of the Most Noble Order of the Garter.
explanation.definitionFit: A band round the leg keeps a stocking up; one in the Order of the Garter, Britain's senior order of knighthood, wears this badge.

parts.note: not the town or room where he composed it, but the place in a printed book where a play's name is written

explanation.surface: A question about where the Bard sat when he wrote his tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks for a place of composition; the answer is the leaf at the front of the book where the play's name appears.
explanation.definitionFit: The opening leaf of a book carries its name and author, where the words King Lear would be printed.

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means the letters are read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: la is French for the
a tot is a small child

explanation.surface: A sum of money is paid to bring up a child from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' reads as bringing up a child, but turns LATOT upwards to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An amount reached by adding is a whole or aggregate.

clue.text: I left a Greek writer for this Latin poet

indicators.note: left means departed, so the letter I goes out of the writer's name

parts.note: Lucian of Samosata was a satirist who wrote in Greek

explanation.surface: A Roman poet replaces a Greek author on someone's reading list.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I left' reads as a first-person confession but means the letter I is dropped from LUCIAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucan wrote the Pharsalia, an epic on the civil war between Caesar and Pompey, in Latin.

clue.text: Fisherman's basket holds many a piece of his tackle

parts.note: C, the Roman numeral for a hundred, stands for many
a reel is part of an angler's tackle, winding the line

explanation.surface: An angler's basket contains plenty of his fishing gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holds' is only a link here, although the surface makes the basket seem to hold the gear.
explanation.definitionFit: A wicker basket for carrying caught fish is the angler's traditional container.

explanation.surface: Someone is giving careful study to a sculpture by Rodin.
explanation.walkthrough: Rodin's sculpture La Pensee is known in English by this name, a sister piece to The Thinker.
explanation.definitionFit: Careful reflection on something is deliberation, and Rodin's marble head La Pensee translates as the same word.

clue.text: There's a clue staring you in the face for her

indicators.text: clue staring you in the face
indicators.note: the clue tells us the answer is right in front of us, spelt out by the opening words

explanation.surface: Someone points out that an obvious hint about a woman is right in front of you.
explanation.walkthrough: The first two words, ignoring the apostrophe, spell out a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's first name is defined simply by a female pronoun.

clue.text: Modern invention needs substantial backing — second investment

indicators.note: an investment here is a clothing or enclosing, so one letter is wrapped inside
backing means going backwards, so the word for substantial is read in reverse

parts.note: something real is substantial, solid

explanation.surface: A new invention requires plenty of financial support and a second round of funding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' and 'investment' look like financial terms; 'backing' reverses REAL to LAER, and 'investment' puts S inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The light-amplifying device was a mid-twentieth-century discovery, a recent technological breakthrough.

explanation.surface: A question about the colour associated with a prince who plays sport.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep bright hue is so named; a blue is someone who represented Oxford or Cambridge at sport, so a regal one is fancifully this.
